item.title: Patient-Level Reassessment of Breast Raman Spectroscopy: Data Leakage and Limits of Subtype Classification
item.description: Reliable interpretation of Raman spectra from breast tissue requires evaluation on patients absent from model training. We reanalysed a public ex vivo dataset comprising 641 spectra, 80 tissue samples and 71 donors to assess the effect of validation design on breast cancer classification. In a GNU Octave reproduction of the deposited analysis, an indexing statement caused an average of 56% of testfold spectra also to be selected for training. With the original and corrected indexing operations, four-class support-vector-machine accuracy was 87.6% and 59.1%, respectively; the reproduction used an approximate kernel-scale setting rather than the original MATLAB heuristic. Under donor-disjoint nested validation, five classifiers achieved 55–60% four-class accuracy, with invasive lobular carcinoma sensitivity of only 6–15%. Cancer-versus-normal classification remained more robust (support vector machine accuracy 90.0%; donor-bootstrap 95% confidence interval 83.8–95.3%). A fixed-pipeline analysis gave four-class accuracies of 81.7%, 77.9%, 60.9% and 62.1% when folds were formed at the spectrum, measurement-point, sample and donor levels, respectively. A bandresolved variance decomposition indicated that donor identity accounted for the largest share of within-class variance at the carotenoid bands (1157 and 1525 cm-1; 58–63%), whereas class information was concentrated at the phenylalanine band (1004 cm-1). Donor-level band ratios differed between cancer and normal tissue but not between DCIS and invasive lobular carcinoma. Adding the highwavenumber region, varying preprocessing, or increasing the number of lobular carcinoma training donors from about 2 to 8 did not raise lobular carcinoma sensitivity above 25%. In a simulation of the measurement chain with real fluorescence backgrounds and Poisson shot noise, donor-shared backgrounds and collection gains produced little optimism after preprocessing, whereas donor-specific tissue chemistry did. Donor-separated conformal calibration yielded 91.0% empirical marginal coverage for the four-class task at a nominal 90% target, but coverage was lower for invasive subtypes; class-conditional calibration equalised coverage across classes but returned large prediction sets. These findings identify substantial validation sensitivity in this dataset and underline the need for patient-level evaluation, reproducible code and classspecific uncertainty reporting.

item.title: Ultrasound-Controlled Activation of Tetrazine-TCO Click-to-release Chemistry Through Sonochemical Oxidation of Dihydrotetrazine
item.description: External control over click chemistry offers opportunities for the spatiotemporal regulation of bioorthogonal ligation and cleavage, but the limited tissue penetration of light constrains photoactivated approaches. Herein, we introduce a new mechanistic approach to ultrasound-controlled click chemistry based on the direct sonochemical oxidation of dihydrotetrazine (DHTz) precursors. The precursors require no additional cleavable masking group, and low-intensity therapeutic ultrasound activates their oxidation through sonochemically generated hydroxyl radicals without the need for added sensitizers. A pyridinyl-substituted precursor, DHTz2, exhibits limited background oxidation and efficient sonochemical activation, while the resulting tetrazine product shows good stability under ultrasound exposure. The ultrasound-activated tetrazine readily undergoes ligation reactions with TCOs, including a TCO-DOX conjugate in which a bioorthogonal click-to-release cascade releases free DOX and restores its cytotoxic activity against cancer cells. Importantly, ultrasound applied through a chicken breast tissue barrier remains effective in triggering bioorthogonal click-to-release and activating the prodrug. This work establishes a new mechanistic approach that couples the fundamental sonochemistry of acoustic cavitation with the selective activation of click chemistry and bioorthogonal cleavage, providing a new platform for the remote, non-optical control of bioorthogonal ligation and cargo release using tissue-penetrating biomedical ultrasound.

item.title: Chemoselective Formylation of an Amine-Functionalized Nucleotide Diphosphate Sugar under Diphosphate-Compatible Conditions
item.description: We report the synthesis of a nucleotide diphosphate 4-amino sugar and its late-stage, chemoselective formylation to the corresponding formamide under conditions compatible with highly polar and sensitive, diphosphate substrates. Uridine diphosphate-4-deoxy-4-amino-α-L-arabinose (UDP-Ara4N) was prepared via a convergent phosphate coupling strategy. Selective Nformylation was achieved with formyl–pivalic mixed anhydride under Schotten–Baumann conditions, providing UDP-4-deoxy-4formamido-α-L-arabinose (UDP-Ara4FN, 72%). These results demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple nucleophilic functionalities, chemoselective amine functionalization can be achieved on fully deprotected NDP amino sugars, providing a practical approach to accessing functionalized nucleotide sugar analogues.

item.title: Surface-Induced Constraint Release in Confined Polymer Films: A Computational Phenomenological Study
item.description: Thin polymer films exhibit thickness-dependent viscoelastic behavior attributed to enhanced segmental mobility near free surfaces, a phenomenon recently linked to surface-induced constraint release (SICR) in entangled polymer melts. While self-consistent theoretical treatments of this mechanism exist, computationally lightweight phenomenological models that isolate the role of specific structural assumptions remain comparatively underexplored. This work showcases a developed closed-form, depth-resolved generalized Maxwell model in which local relaxation times are derived from a depth-dependent entanglement molecular weight profile, motivated by reptation scaling (tau~Z^3.4) and literature-reported surface entanglement enhancement ratios. With this framework, we directly compare two assumptions for combining depth-dependent relaxation behavior into an effective film modulus: a depth-independent linear superposition, and an entanglement-coupled, double-reptation-inspired mixing rule. Holding the underlying relaxation-time profile identical between both models, we find that the choice of coupling mechanism alters the predicted storage modulus by up to ~40%, with the divergence peaking at an intermediate film thickness rather than increasing monotonically as films thin. This work shows that the peak location is associated with, though not fully predicted by, the frequency-dependent heterogeneity of local relaxation times across the film. These results indicate that depth-coupling assumptions in phenomenological thin-film rheology models are not a minor implementation detail, but materially and non-trivially shape predicted thickness-dependent behavior, with implications for how such models should be constructed and interpreted going forward.

item.title: Computational Analysis of Competing Reduction Pathways in the Asymmetric Transfer Hydrogenation of 2-Alkenylquinolines
item.description: Two competing reduction pathways can deliver a single stereochemical outcome. This computational study reveals that within an achiral TFA model, the reduction of 2-alkenylquinolines can begin through nearly isoenergetic 1,4-hydride transfer to either the quinoline ring or the alkenyl side chain. The resulting sequences are proposed to converge on a common prochiral iminium intermediate. Furthermore, analysis of the final chiral phosphoric acid-controlled 1,2-hydride transfer predicts the preferential formation of the experimentally observed major enantiomer.

item.title: Lattice Evolution and Proton Positioning in Hydrogen Molybdenum Bronzes under Pressure
item.description: Hydrogen molybdenum bronzes (HxMoO3) are mixed-valence transition metal oxides whose structural and electronic properties are strongly influenced by their proton behavior. Despite their extensive study under ambient conditions, their structural evolution under compression remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the high-pressure structural behavior of three hydrogen molybdenum bronzes using synchrotron-based powder X-ray and neutron diffraction. Pressure induces structural phase transitions in all three compounds, yet each materials’ evolution is distinct, suggesting a coupling between hydrogen location/concentration and framework stress response. The bronze with the lowest reduction and proton incorporation level (x ~ 0.36, Type I) exhibits a compression pathway similar to that of α-MoO3, whereas at higher hydrogenation levels (x ~ 0.95, Type II; x ~ 1.68, Type III), distinct pressure-dependent changes in bulk modulus reveal altered elastic response during compression. Complementary in situ neutron diffraction measurements on D0.36MoO3 directly locate the hydrogen atom at an equatorial oxygen. Upon compression to 7.8 ± 1.5 GPa, the local hydrogen environment becomes increasingly constrained, exhibiting significant deviation of the O–D···O angle from 180° and shortening of the D···O distance by ca. 0.3 Å. These results establish the structural response of hydrogen molybdenum bronzes to high pressure and demonstrate how proton incorporation governs framework distortions and compressibility.

item.title: Examining Copper Lead Surface Alloys as Potential Catalysts for the Electrochemical Carbon Dioxide Reduction
item.description: The conversion of carbon dioxide into useful or environmentally benign chemicals is currently of great interest to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Yet in spite of numerous efforts effective CO2 conversion still presents a considerable challenge. One of the most promising catalysts for CO2 conversion to hydrocarbons is copper. In this computational study based on density functional theory we have addressed bimetallic PbCu catalysts to elucidate whether there are synergistic catalytic effects through the alloying of Cu with Pb, as suggested experimentally. Using a well-established descriptor for the catalytic activity based on hydrogen and CO adsorption energies, we analyzed the potential catalytic activity of PbCu surface alloys on copper. The computational results confirm that through a combination of strain and ligand effects these surface alloys can act as favorable catalysts for valuable hydrocarbons.

item.title: From a Tight-Binding Hessian to an AMBER Iron-Sulfur Site: A Rubredoxin Stress Test
item.description: Parameterized bonded metal sites represent the lowest cost option for molecular dynamics (MD) studies of metalloproteins. However, their quality depends entirely upon the underlying quantum computation and validation. Here, we have asked whether it is possible to generate reliable AMBER force field parameters for a rubredoxin Fe-S4 active site from an extended tight-binding (xTB-family) Hessian. The Hessian derived from a 49-atom cluster was projected using the Seminario method to give parameters for Fe-S and S-Fe-S interactions. The active site was then solvated explicitly, and three 100 ns trajectories were generated. The entire process was performed end-to-end. The trajectories all maintained the protein secondary structure (RMSD Cα mean 1.2-1.6 Å). Two of the trajectories maintained a tetrahedral iron site, while one did not. At around 31.4 ns, the mean Fe-S bond length increased from 2.41 to 2.63 Å, and the deviation from tetrahedral geometry increased from 8.8 to 43.5°. Two cysteine sulfur atoms also approached each other to a bond length of 2.04 Å. None of these issues were identified using global measures. The parameters are reported along with the cause of failure, likely reasons, and missing provenance, meaning this is merely a proof of concept, not a validated force field.

item.title: A Cellular Sheaf Model for Aromaticity in Discrete Molecular Systems
item.description: Aromaticity underpins molecular stability in fields ranging from pharmaceuticals to organic semiconductors, yet existing prediction methods are either too computationally costly for large-scale screening or too empirically restricted for broad applicability. This work introduces the molecular sheaf, a cellular sheaf model free of empirical parameters for chemical bonding that generalizes standard molecular graph theory. From this the frontier eigengap Δ_F is derived as a spectral approximation of the HOMO-LUMO gap requiring only molecular topology and electron count. Δ_F correctly classifies the aromaticity and antiaromaticity of the full annulene series, including benzene and cyclobutadiene, exactly recovering Hückel theory for regular hydrocarbon systems. At scale, it accounts for 62.5% of the variance in DFT HOMO-LUMO gaps across 17,523 structurally diverse polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and 21.7% across 52,000 heteroaromatic systems, with the reduction reflecting the deliberate cost of parameter freedom. This confirms that aromatic character can be approximated from molecular connectivity and electron count alone, suggesting that cellular sheaves offer a largely unexplored mathematical framework for the modeling of chemical bonding and structure. All calculations run at under 1 ms per molecule, over seven orders of magnitude faster than corresponding DFT calculations. The molecular sheaf thus also enables rapid, parameter-free pre-screening of aromatic character from structural data alone.

item.title: Systematic Evaluation of Mixture-Design for Multi-Oxide Magnesium Aluminosilicate Glass Development: Model Comparison, Modifier Interactions, and Predictive Limitations
item.description: A constrained ternary mixture design (Design of Experiments, DoE) was applied to four magnesium aluminosilicate (MAS) glass series to evaluate the predictive capability of Scheffé mixture polynomials for the specific Young’s modulus (spE = E/ρ), the key figure of merit for lightweight glass-fibre reinforcements. Two base compositions (V, Al2O3-rich; T, MgO-rich) were each modified with a 14 wt.% Y2O3–ZnO–CeO2 or La2O3–ZnO–CeO2 block. Linear, quadratic and special-cubic models were fitted to ten design points per series and ranked by R2, R2(adj) and the leave-one-out coefficient R2(pred). Three distinct regimes emerge: the V-series requires a special-cubic model with a dominant ternary Y2O3·ZnO·CeO2 term (β = −47.2, p = 0.001; R2(pred) = 97 %); the T-series is strictly linear (R2(pred) = 55 %), higher orders overfitting; and both La-series show a significant La2O3·CeO2 interaction absent in their Y-analogues. Three additive property models (Makishima–Mackenzie, an extended variant, and Yamane–Sakaino) deviate systematically from measured spE (absolute errors 6.9–12.2 × 106 N·m·kg-1, negative R2), most strongly where DoE detects interactions. The study delineates where additive approaches suffice, where binary synergy dominates, and where genuinely ternary cooperative effects must be resolved.

item.title: Macroscopic two-dimensional sheets by chemically triggered self-assembly.
item.description: Bottom-up self-assembly of two-dimensional (2D) sheets is rare. We present in situ reaction driven self-assembly for semithroughput synthesis of imine based 2D materials. Easily tuneable molecular structures and reaction kinetics allow for up to seven sheet forming systems.

item.title: Making Complete-Basis-Set Extrapolation Visible: A Spreadsheet-Based Activity for Upper-Division Computational Chemistry
item.description: Complete-basis-set (CBS) extrapolation is widely used to estimate electronic energies beyond finite-basis calculations. However, students may encounter it primarily as a formula or automated correction, which obscures how a CBS value is constructed from a sequence of finite-basis energies. We describe a scaffolded Excel activity that makes this process visible by linking energy tables, component extrapolations, and convergence plots. Students first examine Hartree-Fock and correlation-energy convergence in the hydrogen chloride heteronuclear diatomic molecule, compare CBS estimates obtained from alternative extrapolation choices, and then apply the same workflow to the hydrogen fluoride molecule HF. The activity culminates in the calculation and justification of CBS-derived atomization energies and comparison to experiment. This activity is implemented in an upper-division computational chemistry course, and was evaluated through a pre-activity quiz and rubric-based analysis of completed student work. In general, students executed the component extrapolations successfully, yet evaluating sensitivity and justifying a final reported value proved more challenging. The activity offers a transparent and adaptable approach for teaching students to evaluate, rather than merely obtain, computational chemistry results.

item.title: Inverse magneto-ionics enhances oxygen evolution reaction
item.description: Applying magnetic fields to electrodes has been reported to enhance electrochemical reactions, leading to numerous studies and the hypothesis that externally applied magnetic fields manipulate direct spin exchange at the electrode–electrolyte interface to control reaction kinetics. However, a closer analysis suggests that this mechanism is unlikely to play a significant role, whereas the influence of magnetic gradient forces on ion migration is well established. Here, we provide experimental evidence supporting the latter mechanism for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) on nickel. Moderate magnetic fields increase the electrochemical current density by up to 20%. For pristine samples, the enhancement is both field-and time-dependent. We demonstrate that the magnetic field effect does not arise from direct spin alignment at the electrode surface or from the magnetic domain structure of the underlying ferromagnetic film. Instead, the external magnetic field indirectly enhances the electrochemical performance through magnetic gradient forces that promote the growth of the electrocatalytically active nickel oxyhydroxide surface layer by driving the exsolution of paramagnetic Ni species during the OER. With the structure of the passivation layer of Ni and its evolution being common in similar d-metal (alloy) electrode materials, the magnetic field effect by ion migration is likely to be generally valid.

item.title: Enantio-Complementary Synthesis of Atropisomeric C–N Biaryl Amines via Imine Reductase-Mediated Dynamic Kinetic Resolution
item.description: C–N axially chiral biaryl amines constitute privileged scaffolds in drug discovery and asymmetric catalysis, yet they remain synthetically challenging due to low rotational barriers and inherent conformational flexibility. While biocatalysis presents an attractive avenue for constructing chiral amines, the lack of mirror-image enzymes has historically limited access to all stereoisomers. Here, we develop an unconventional biocatalytic platform leveraging dynamic kinetic reductive amination to synthesize C–N axially chiral biaryl amines in both enantiomeric forms. Through systematic screening and enzyme engineering, we achieved the synthesis of diverse aryl indole atropisomers with exceptional yields and enantioselectivities (up to 99% yield and 99% ee). Strikingly, we uncovered a unique stereo-divergent behavior wherein a single biocatalyst switches its stereochemical outcome solely by toggling the amine partner between alkylamines and arylamines. Mechanistic investigations using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations unveiled the origins of the high enantioselectivity, the substrate-dependent stereochemical reversal, and the catalytic enhancement imparted by a single point mutation. This study not only provides a robust platform for accessing elusive C–N axial chirality but also exemplifies the synergy between enzyme engineering and computational modeling in achieving stereo-divergent synthesis.

item.title: Memory effects in active droplets
item.description: Marangoni-driven self-propelled droplets have attracted considerable attention as a platform to study active soft matter and collective behavior. The speed of active drops is generally assumed to be determined by instantaneous diameter and solubilization rate, which together dictate the spontaneously generated interfacial tension gradients across the drop surface and induce propulsion; the history of the droplet has not before been considered. Here, we report that active droplets can exhibit a type of memory wherein the temporal history of the droplet, particularly the starting diameter, influences the droplet speed. For example, two droplets of identical instantaneous diameter in the same local chemical environment can exhibit dramatically different instantaneous velocities depending upon their initial diameter. This effect is observed for a range of droplet oils and common ionic surfactants. The relationships between drop diameter, velocity, and solubilization rate were examined for several ionic and nonionic surfactants and suggest that droplet motility only is present when solubilization is interfacially limited, as opposed to diffusion limited. Oil droplets in ionic surfactant solutions also undergo a transition from motile to non-motile, where the diameter at the transitionary point depends upon initial drop diameter. We hypothesize that this memory behavior may result from an interfacial phase transition, as hinted at by observed visual deformations on drop interfaces under some circumstances. We believe this work provides insight as to how memory may be imparted in active droplet systems, highlights the importance of non-equilibrium phenomena in active materials, and offers valuable insights for the design of adaptive, dynamic droplet systems.

item.title: Transformation of Nitrogenous Compounds in Water Microdroplets
item.description: Microdroplets drive small-molecule activation reactions that are difficult in bulk solution. Recent studies have demonstrated that microdroplets activate inert N2 under ambient conditions to generate multiple nitrogencontaining compounds. However, there are still many controversial issues regarding the transformation of nitrogencontaining compounds in water microdroplets. Here, we combine online high-resolution mass spectrometry on two instrument platforms with 15N and 18O labeling to investigate nitrogen-containing species in pneumatically generated water microdroplets. Ammonium-containing water clusters, nitrite, and nitrate ions were detected on both instruments, whereas a signal assigned to NO+ was observed only on the Agilent 6224 TOF MS. Nebulization with

item.title: Limitations of Impedance Spectroscopy in Detecting Interfacial Contact Quality – Insights from Metal Anode Dissolution in Solid-State Batteries
item.description: Reliable assessment of buried solid–solid interfaces is essential for understanding and improving electrochemical devices including solid-state batteries. Electrical measurements such as electrochemical impedance spectroscopy provide an attractive (operando) diagnostic but probe interfacial contact only indirectly through its influence on charge transport. Consequently, the extent to which interfacial morphology can be inferred from the electrical response remains unclear. Here, we use 3D electric network simulations to study how interfacial morphology governs the impedance detectability of non-ideal contacts at constriction-dominated interfaces. The resulting general principles are discussed using metal dissolution at interfaces with fast charge-transfer kinetics as a representative case. We show that no universal detection threshold exists. Instead, detectability depends on the remaining contact area, the lateral distribution of contact and non-contact regions, and the sample thickness. In limiting cases with small, finely distributed pores, contact losses exceeding 90% may remain largely undetectable, whereas localized contact loss produces pronounced impedance features at substantially higher remaining contact areas. These findings reveal a morphology-induced diagnostic blind spot in impedance-based interface analysis and demonstrate that the absence of a measurable interface signal does not necessarily imply intimate or stable interfacial contact. This diagnostic blind spot therefore challenges the reliability of conclusions and material parameters derived from electrical measurements without independent knowledge of the underlying interface morphology.

item.title: PyFMO: A Python Framework for Fragment Molecular Orbital Calculations
item.description: The fragment molecular orbital (FMO) method enables quantum chemical calculations on large biomolecular systems and provides interaction energies between their fragments. Its further development and wider adoption would benefit from software in which new methods can be prototyped rapidly, every stage of a calculation can be inspected, and both developers and users can contribute to extending the method. Here we present PyFMO, a Python framework for FMO calculations that uses PySCF as its electronic-structure backend. An FMO calculation is expressed as a pipeline of interchangeable steps that share a common context, and all results are collected in a serializable container that can be analyzed independently of the calculation. PyFMO supports Hartree–Fock, density functional theory, and correlated methods at the FMO1–FMO3 levels, as well as continuum solvation and pair interaction energy decomposition analysis (PIEDA), including directional charge-transfer and three-body terms. Proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, and glycoproteins are fragmented automatically using rule-based substructure matching. For production calculations, density fitting accelerates both the fragment calculations and the evaluation of electrostatic couplings, while node-level shared memory and cost-model-based load balancing are designed for execution on platforms ranging from laptops to high-performance computing clusters. Benchmarks and an application to a theophylline-binding RNA aptamer, where PIEDA provides a detailed picture of the ligand recognition, demonstrate these capabilities. By combining the flexibility of Python with the performance required for large systems, PyFMO makes the development, testing, and application of new FMO methods for biomolecular problems accessible to a broad community.

item.title: Incorporating Polarization into ML/MM Endpoint Calculations for Protein–Ligand Affinity Ranking
item.description: Endpoint free-energy calculations combine low computational cost with reasonable accuracy and are widely used to rank protein–ligand affinities, yet describing charge polarization in these calculations remains a challenge. Here we introduce a machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) framework that incorporates polarizationcorrected mechanical embedding (PCME) and electrostatic embedding (EE) into endpoint calculations, using binding-state-and conformation-dependent ML charges in both the gas-phase energy and polar solvation terms. On a benchmark of 15 targets from the JACS and Merck sets, the PCME and EE routes of ML/MM-PBSA rank affinities better than classical MM-PBSA, raising the median Spearman ρ from 0.216 to 0.343 and 0.329, respectively, at an acceptable computational cost. A charge-source control and the analysis of a representative PTP1B complex show how conformationdependent ML charges resolve asymmetric local electrostatic environments and contribute to the improved ranking of ML/MM-PBSA(PCME) over MM-PBSA. By incorporating charge redistribution into both interaction and solvation energies, this work provides a practical ML/MM endpoint framework for protein–ligand affinity ranking and analysis of the underlying electrostatic contributions.

item.title: Analytical Evidence for Assessing Plastic Pyrolysis Oils as Steam Cracker Feedstocks
item.description: Qualification of plastic pyrolysis oils for steam cracking requires measurements that connect product recovery, composition, and operating performance. This critical narrative review examines 96 selected full-text publications through reconstructed comparisons of analytical coverage, calibration, uncertainty, and material inventories. In individual studies, GC-assigned species represented approximately 11% of total silicon, and olefin estimates differed by 7.4 percentage points despite a pooled coefficient of determination above 0.99. A cracking comparison showed approximately 2.4 times the coke formation rate for an untreated-oil/naphtha blend alongside a small ethylene-yield gain. A claim–evidence framework connects these findings to purification, usableproduct recovery, and feed qualification. Priorities are paired bulk and species measurements, independently measured phase recoveries, matrix-relevant validation, and matched upgrading and cracking tests. The synthesis provides guidance for process assessment while distinguishing results for tested streams and conditions from industrial operating reliability.

item.title: Revealing the role of Li content on the structural stability of textured LiCoO2 battery electrodes along fast diffusing <11x> directions
item.description: Facile ion transport in layered battery cathode systems require (11x) terminating facets. However, the facets that provide accelerated transport also amplify deleterious phase transitions and chemical reactions. The coupling between initial intercalant ion content (nominal lithium-ion stoichiometry), ionic mobility and phase transformations along the fastest diffusing facets remain understudied. Here, the coupling is elucidated using electrodeposited highly textured <11x>||(sample normal direction, ND) LiCoO2 (LCO) electrodes with controlled texture, facet presentation, and initial lithium content. Contrary to powdered systems with untextured particles, here we show that minute variations in lithium content drive distinct interphase formation at (110) terminating facets and impact ion diffusivity in cathodes possessing identical <110>IIND texture, indicating the unique importance of control of lithium content in highly oriented systems. While Lithium-poor <110>IIND LCO cathodes provide initial good ion diffusivity, they exhibit accelerated interfacially originated degradation along <110> directions via rapid rocksalt formation. Lithium-rich <110>IIND LCO electrodes exhibit elevated interfacial degradation due to the poorly conducting Li2CO3 on the surface. Lithium-balanced textured LCO electrodes suppress kinetically driven degradation pathways, even at (110) terminating facets, and provide both good ion diffusivity and structural stability. The dual control of lithium content and crystallographic orientation along the fastest diffusing directions provided by the textured electrodeposited cathodes enables deterministic design of energy-dense cathodes with good ion transport kinetics and low surface reactivity, both in thin and thick electrode formats, a combination which is difficult to achieve in untextured slurry systems presenting a range of surface facets.

item.title: From Dynamic Frustration to Steric Trapping: The Microscopic Mechanism of a Monotropic Phase Transition
item.description: The atomic-level mechanisms governing solvent-driven single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) topotactic transitions are notoriously difficult to capture, as transient, symmetry-broken intermediates (Z′ > 1) rarely survive structural collapse. Here, we map the complete molecular trajectory of a cooperative solid-state transition within a heavily hydrated di-iron-µ-O-2'-cytidine monophosphate complex, [Fe2(µ-O)(TPA)2(2′-CMP)](ClO4)2·xH2O. By tuning crystallization kinetics, we isolated two distinct solvatomorphic pathways: a thermodynamically stable Z′ = 1 phase and an elusive, kinetically trapped Z′ = 2 interphase. In the reversible Z′ = 1 pathway, the host lattice maintains volumetric invariance across 120–298 K while undergoing a continuous, entropically driven internal hydrogen-bond toggle. Conversely, the metastable Z′ = 2 solvatomorph physically bridges the transition pathway by co-crystallizing incompatible 'open' and 'closed' conformations of two chemical latches. These two chemical latches are the two kind of hydrogen bonds-the cytosine C6-H6 to sugar C5′-hydroxyl oxygen (C6-H6···O5′) and sugar C3′-hydroxyl to phosphate P=O oxygen (O3′-H3′···O=P) contacts within a single asymmetric unit. Fine-sliced variable-temperature X-ray diffraction (150–310 K) reveals that prior to collapse, one of the molecules in the asymmetric unit, acts as a dynamic shock absorber. This molecule reversibly breaking and reforming of its C6···O5′ latch (3.22-3.65 Å) drives a ~ 31° glycosidic swing and bimodal occupancy shifting, while the competing O3′···O=P contact contracts (3.11 to 2.90 Å) to buffer thermal strain. Crossing a 280 K kinetic threshold triggers an abrupt, monotropic 50% volumetric collapse (Z′ = 2 → Z′ = 1), subjecting the merged nucleotide site to severe structural shock before permanently clamping both frustrated latches into a sterically jammed, statically disordered state (C6···O5′at 3.26 Å; O3′···O=P at 2.76 Å). Strikingly, the sheer mechanical force driven by this frustrated latch clamping violently expels few crystallized water near the freezing point of bulk water (273-280 K)- while the collapsed matrix retains permanent microporosity to dynamically resorb and order guest water upon cooling.

item.title: Decision stability of a default docking pipeline: a seed, box-placement, and protomer audit on LIT-PCBA MTORC1
item.description: Agentic and automated drug-discovery workflows increasingly call molecular docking as a black-box subroutine and act on its ranked output, typically from a single run under software defaults. We ask a narrow, operational question: if the same default pipeline is re-run with a different random seed, a slightly displaced search box, or a different input protomer, which decisions-the top-k compounds a downstream agent would advanceactually change? Using AutoDock Vina 1.2.7 on the LIT-PCBA MTORC1 target (PDB 4jsx) with a fixed, score-blind panel of 60 ligands (20 actives, 40 inactives), we predeclared the decision rule and the seed and box-placement perturbation axes against a baseline, added a protomer arm whose selection criterion was amended during execution (disclosed with dates), and compared top-12 decision sets as symmetric differences (exits and entries), Jaccard indices, and binary decision changes, with pose quality checked by PoseBusters against the exact receptor used for docking. A positive control (redocking the co-crystallized ligand, symmetry-corrected RMSD 0.647 Å) validated the setup. Changing only the random seed replaced 3 of 12 top-12 members (6/60 binary decisions changed); a 2 Å box shift along x replaced 2, along y replaced 4; protomer changes at pH 7.0 replaced none. Eight ligands accounted for all flips, and the single PoseBustersinvalid pose was also a recurrent flipper. A threeseed majority-vote consensus cost 3× compute, dropped the invalid recurrent flipper, and still disagreed with every individual run; we report it as a priced mitigation with measured residual disagreement, not as certified stabilization. All results concern decision repeatability only: nothing here establishes that any decision set is correct, and a consensus can stabilize a wrong answer. All code, inputs, checkpoints, and negative results are provided in an accompanying archive prepared for the author; no public release has been made.

item.title: Martini 3 Coarse-Grained Models for Steroid Hormones
item.description: Steroid hormones are central to the development, metabolism, homeostasis and reproduction of animals and have been the subject of many evolutionary, ecotoxicological and human health studies. Coarse-grain molecular dynamics (CG MD) simulations are a powerful tool to study the structural and dynamic behavior of steroid hormones and their interactions. Here, we expand the capabilities of the widely used Martini 3 CG framework by parameterizing and validating a set of 20 steroid hormone models — including both endogenous and synthetic molecules — to enable their study across diverse targets, systems, and fields of interest.Hormone parameterization followed Martini 3 guidelines, while leveraging the similarities with the parent cholesterol molecule, for which a Martini 3 model is available. Notably, we were able to base our parameterization on the hundreds of experimental structures in the protein data bank that contain steroid hormones, instead of relying on atomistic simulations as is typical with Martini.The parameterized models match to within 5% target molecular volumes, and recover the overall hydrophobicity trend of the hormones, although higher hydrophobicities tended to be overestimated. In free simulations of protein-hormone systems the experimentally known binding poses could be recovered for 89% of the cases, indicating a successful parameterization also from a functional standpoint. Since several Martini 3 protein models were tested, we also incidentally show that the flexibility of the OLIVES and GōMartini models makes them best suited for this type of protein–ligand recognition. Finally, models were validated in interaction with membranes by comparison to reference atomistic data.We expect that the availability of our fully validated Martini 3 CG steroid hormone models will contribute to new studies, collaborations, and applications across different scientific fields.

item.title: The Evolution of Electronic Structure in Conjugated Molecules Revealed by Mixed-Reference Spin-Flip Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory and Density-Based Analyses: II. Polyacenes
item.description: Large conjugated molecules feature small gaps between occupied and virtual orbital spaces, which results in complex electronic structure patterns in their low-lying states. These orbital near-degeneracies also challenge quantum chemistry methods. Mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT (MRSF-TDDFT) and density-matrix-based analyses provide useful tools to interrogate electronic structure in large conjugated molecules. This paper investigates one such family—polyacenes. Following our recent study of the ground and low-lying excited states of all-trans polyenes, we track this evolution from benzene to dodecacene using MRSF-TDDFT and densitymatrix-based analyses. In polyacenes, the ground state acquires diradical character as the number of rings increases, while the doubly excited state dominated by the HOMO2 → LUMO2 configuration drops steeply in energy and falls below the La state between nonacene and decacene. MRSF-TDDFT reproduces the experimental La/Lb crossing, which standard linear-response TDDFT misses, and gives singlettriplet gaps close to high-level wave-function benchmarks and singlet-fission energetics consistent with experiment. The analyses show that La remains predominantly singly excited throughout the series and we attribute the strong decrease in its oscillator strength to the growing diradical character of the ground state. The doubly excited state evolves from mixed character in naphthalene, similar to the 2 1Ag− state of the polyenes, to a nearly closed-shell doubly excited state in pentacene and hexacene, and finally to a state with natural orbital occupations resembling those of the ground state in the longest acenes. item.title: Literature-Scale Mössbauer Data Enable Prediction, Electronic-State Interpretation, and Chemical Insight in Molecular Iron Chemistry
item.description: Experimental spectroscopy is central to molecular characterization, yet conventional quantitative analysis often compresses rich structural and electronic information into a few calculated observables, leaving much of the experimental context and expert interpretation reported in the literature underused. Here, using molecular 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy as a representative case, we reconstructed more than 300 publications into FeMössDB, a site-resolved dataset containing 502 Fe complexes and 624 Fe sites with linked structural, experimental, and interpretive information. Using FeMössDB, we developed FeMössML for three complementary aspects of Mössbauer analysis: isomer-shift/quadrupole-splitting (IS/QS) prediction, electronic-state interpretation, and analysis of structure–state–spectroscopy relationships. FeMössML reduces IS/QS prediction errors by about 30% relative to a single global density functional theory (DFT) calibration and achieves cross-validated electronic-state accuracies of up to 92%, while correctly assigning several challenging low-valent and electronically delocalized Fe complexes. Feature analysis further recovers established relationships between Mössbauer parameters and oxidation state, spin state, and Fe–L geometry from the literature-scale dataset. FeMössML can also use geometries rapidly generated by Universal Models for Atoms (UMA) or experimental X-ray structures without target-specific DFT hyperfine calculations, reducing wall-clock time by more than three orders of magnitude. More broadly, this work points to a new paradigm for spectroscopic analysis, moving from compound-by-compound quantum-chemical calculation and expert interpretation toward literature-scale reuse of experimental and interpretive data for prediction, interpretation, and systematic relationship analysis.

item.title: Bringing coupled‑cluster theory to the strong-correlation frontier
item.description: Accurate prediction of molecular electronic energies is essential yet remains challenging for strongly correlated systems, where conventional coupled-cluster (CC) methods break down. Here we present a generalized valence bond-based block-correlated coupled‑cluster (GVB-BCCC) framework to overcome this limitation. In contrast to standard CC approaches built upon a single-determinant reference, our method employs a multi‑determinantal GVB reference paired with a cluster operator that consistently captures both static and dynamic electron correlation effects, while retaining computational efficiency comparable to single-reference CC theory. With its O(N⁷) scaling, GVB‑BCCC delivers chemical accuracy for global potential energy surfaces, reaction barriers, and singlet‑triplet gaps across diverse biradicals and transition-metal complexes. GVB-BCCC thereby enables routine, black-box quantum-chemical predictions for a wide variety of strongly correlated systems, ranging from transition-metal catalysts and organic radicals to functional molecular materials.

item.title: Randomized PEG-Based Polycarbonate Micelles with PEG-like Stealth Properties and Biodistribution
item.description: The increase in anti-PEG antibodies (APAs) as well as PEG-related adverse effects have questioned the benefits of PEGylated nanotherapeutics. Growing awareness of the safety and efficacy of PEGylation has prompted research into countermeasures, including alternative polymers. Among these, randomized PEG (rPEG) was established as a fundamentally new approach that preserves the polyether structure while preventing antibody recognition through isomerization. Here, rPEG was incorporated into polymeric micelles (PMs) for immunodrug delivery to assess its suitability as a PEG replacement. Amphiphilic rPEG polycarbonate block copolymers were synthesized via chain extension using rPEG macroinitiators with primary hydroxy end groups. The respective PMs self-assembled via solvent-exchange evaporation, encapsulating the hydrophobic TLR7/8 agonist CL075 as the immunodrug. rPEG-based PMs demonstrated size distributions and encapsulation efficiencies similar to those of PEG. In vitro assays confirmed that rPEG-PMs had comparable cellular uptake, no cellular toxicity, and similar drug-delivery efficiencies to PEG-PMs. Notably, competitive ELISAs revealed markedly decreased antigenicity of rPEG-PMs towards backbone- and end group-specific APAs. In a fiveday biodistribution study, rPEG-PMs showed whole-body and organ distribution patterns comparable to mPEG-PMs, as would be expected for a stealth polymer. Strikingly, despite the immunostimulatory payload, serum ELISA after a single dose detected anti-rPEG IgM in one of five mice, compared with anti-PEG IgM in three of five mice receiving mPEG-PMs, suggesting lower immunogenic potential for rPEG-PMs, though this remains to be confirmed in repeat-dose studies. Overall, these results position rPEG as a highly promising alternative to PEG for polycarbonate-based PMs and next-generation nanotherapeutics.

item.title: Interaction without an interaction module
item.description: The prevailing way to model a many-body system is to encode every component and then let a module capture interaction. We show that the explicit interaction module is harmful when the number of components increases. We use a simple interaction-carrying encoder that compresses a component’s interaction contribution into its representation, and combine the representations by linear aggregation. This modelling approach is simple in form yet delivers unexpectedly excellent performance: it matches the prevailing explicit route under most conditions and exceeds it when a mixture carries more components than the training set covered. Moreover, an encoder produced this way has a clear advantage over per-component descriptors when it is transferred to a similar task: it greatly reduces the data requirements.

item.title: Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
item.description: The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

item.title: A Coupled Chemo-Mechanical and Life-Cycle Framework for Oyster-Shell-Derived Cementitious Materials in Aggressive Infrastructure Environments
item.description: Oyster-shell powder is promoted as a low-carbon cement substitute, but joint carbon and durability benefits are usually asserted rather than tested. This paper asks when shell-derived concrete (shell replacing cement) delivers a carbon cut with non-inferior service life relative to ordinary Portland cement (OPC) concrete. A coupled hydration–transport–damage–carbon model is run through paired Monte Carlo analysis of a pavement, a dam and a marine culvert. Published data reject the original inert-filler strength model. An effective strength-efficiency coefficient k_f calibrated on one scallop-shell dataset does not generalize to independent oyster-shell data (mean absolute error 0.12 against 0.15 for the inert model; root-mean-square error 0.17 against 0.15), and k_f ranges from -0.40 to 1.36 across four studies, so the primary results use a pooled random-effects distribution. At 25% replacement and constant water-to-binder ratio the median carbon change is −21% with strength 0.88 of OPC; with strength matched it is −15% (P10–P90 −22 to +10%). In the primary configuration (pooled strength-only k_f, sampled diffusivity mapping, OPC reference) the probability of a carbon cut of at least 5% with non-inferior life is at most 0.21 for the pavement, 0.14 for the dam and 0.03 for the marine culvert, and zero against a 50% slag blended cement; other, equally unmeasured transport assumptions give 0.18 to 0.68 for the pavement. All probabilities are conditional scenario results, not empirical probabilities for real infrastructure, and the study is a falsifiable computational screening framework, not a validated service-life model.

item.title: Impedance, admittance or current–voltage? What each measurement really tells about charge transport in deepblue hosts
item.description: Host mobilities are usually quoted from one technique without saying what that technique can actually pin down. Using single-carrier devices of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts, we credit impedance spectroscopy (IS), admittance and steady-state current–voltage (J–V ) data each with what they can fix. Documented rules for point selection, dispersion and transport onset make the published IS mobilities reproducible. Quality-gated admittance pins down the electrostatic state of the films: its ac conductance exceeds the dc conductance of the corresponding device types by up to several hundred times, and no transit feature is resolved in the clean band. Gated J–V sweeps locate a high-slope onset consistent with trap filling under stated assumptions, and the spread between successive sweeps of one device sets a built-in check before hosts are ranked. The result is a constraint map that assigns each technique its role and makes host-transport claims auditable.

item.title: Beyond single numbers: how to choose host materials for deep-blue TADF OLEDs
item.description: Deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) OLEDs stand or fall on their host, yet hosts are still chosen from a handful of single numbers: triplet energy, singlet–triplet gap, frontier levels, glass transition and carrier mobility. We compiled these descriptors for sixteen hosts and cohost components from six chemical families, tracing the source, method and condition behind every value, and find that most are protocol-dependent observables rather than material constants: published triplet energies of one molecule differ by up to 0.12 eV, and five analyses of the same devices place one host’s electron-to-hole mobility ratio anywhere between 0.77 and 3.1. A one-protocol calculation of 50 molecules shows that computed-gap rankings depend on functional choice and require validation against measurement. We review how exciplex-forming, mixed and sensitised hosts share the host’s tasks and what limits operational stability, and propose a minimum reporting standard and a roadmap toward protocol-locked, multi-descriptor host selection.

item.title: How the fruit fly mushroom body can help autonomous materials discovery
item.description: Self-driving laboratories plan well but react slowly: a failing run, finished conversion or odd reading needs a call within seconds, at the instrument. We built that reflex stage by stage from the fruit-fly odor circuit. Raman bands become odor channels; a fixed number of cells fire, keeping shape, not strength. An output compartment learns to stop after one failed and one good run, and keeps learning. In simulated selenization and argon-ion irradiation of 2D semiconductors (20 repeats), one fixed-setting layer made four calls. It needs no retraining over a campaign and its memory does not grow, yet a rare phase from one burst was recognized on an early return. The stop cut flakes lost from 7.75 to 3.55 of 30, level with tuned tools. In a simulator from four published spectra, three flakes gave it slightly lower dose error than an equal-memory raw-spectrum lookup. Ending furnace runs at the instrument lost 0.10 flakes, against 11.0 waiting an assumed 60 s for a planner. Engineered specialists, one per call, are smaller, flag odd readings better and run 24-fold faster. Laboratories can split decisions in two: the planner keeps the recipe; a small fly-circuit layer at each instrument makes the fast calls.

item.title: Same Raw Data, Different Numbers: Locked Analysis Rules Make Film Descriptors of Organic Semiconductors Reproducible
item.description: Optical gaps, Urbach energies, oxidation potentials, surface correlation lengths, diffraction order and thermal transitions are used to rank organic semiconductor films, yet each number is the output of an analysis whose discretionary steps are rarely fixed. Here a protocol card is introduced in which every descriptor is extracted by a locked rule and accepted only if it passes a stated test; otherwise it is reported as “not determined”. Each rule is stress-tested against the choices it fixes. Applied to the archived raw data of three deep-blue phosphine-oxide host films, a free choice of fit window lets the Urbach energy of the same spectra range from 0.21 to 0.94 eV, whereas the locked rule returns 0.22–0.24 eV for all three hosts on glass. The same protocol dependence appears in onset versus peak oxidation potentials, AFM correlation lengths, diffraction baselines, the mass basis of weight-loss temperatures and the functional used for computed orbital energies. Ten locked rules with their stress tests make every reported value auditable and every missing value explicit, and propose a reporting protocol for molecular semiconductor films.

item.title: vibe-qc: expert-directed agentic engineering for scientific software development
item.description: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can implement scientific software, but useful development also requires executable comparisons, inspectable results and a record of scientific decisions. This case study examines the tooling that enables semi-autonomous electronic-structure software development under expert direction. VIBE-QC supplies molecular and periodic calculations; vibe-scheduler queues and manages calculations across clusters and a fleet of workstations; vibe-viewer and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) connect numerical outputs to portable inspection and reproducible figures. Retained development records illustrate how these tools preserve failed attempts, distinguish changes in physical conventions from implementation errors, and separate measured differences from expert-selected acceptance criteria. Publication-specific calculations were run with VIBE-QC 0.18.x and use formaldehyde to connect controlled numerical comparisons with visual inspection; diamond and lithium hydride provide periodic Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) examples with explicit convergence checks. The expert sets the physical problem, selects diagnostic controls and interprets the evidence; AI agents implement and execute those tasks. The resulting account identifies practical requirements for sustained AI-assisted scientific development. It establishes a traceable process within one project, without claiming autonomous scientific judgment or a measured productivity advantage.

item.title: The Meta-Link Rule Revisited: Relaxed Triplets and Non-Radiative Loss Decide Deep-Blue Phosphine-Oxide Hosts
item.description: Deep-blue host design relies on a textbook rule: join the donor and the phosphine-oxide acceptor through a meta-phenylene link to break conjugation and keep the triplet energy high. Tested against experiment, the rule alone does not explain the measured photoluminescence-yield ordering. In a prespecified test on 36 deep-blue emitters, none of the tested radiative descriptors passes all four film-yield ranking criteria, and the meta-linked S1 host and the para-linked S4 host have overlapping apparent radiative-rate brackets yet differ 18-fold in apparent non-radiative rate. One calibrated excited-state protocol, applied to the hosts, their all-meta isomers and emitter pairs, shows that a meta break raises the vertical triplet energy and narrows the singlet–triplet gap, but the gain is lost on relaxation, and the vibronic displacement of the S1 state follows the measured yields. Screens for deep-blue hosts should therefore rank link positions by relaxed triplet energies, estimate non-radiative loss, and read a 1-eV computed gap as a property of locally excited states rather than as evidence against delayed fluorescence.

item.title: Colour-Stable When Heated, Colour-Shifting When Excited: Deep-Blue TADF Hosts Need Vector, Not Scalar, Screening
item.description: Deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) materials are screened by a single figure of meritquantum yield, singlet–triplet gap, colour shift or activation energy—on the assumption that a material robust under one stress is robust under others. Here we show that this assumption fails. For three related phosphineoxide hosts, the host whose emission colour moves least on heating is the one whose colour moves most when the excitation wavelength is changed: an 8-to 17-fold reversal, read directly from instrument chromaticity coordinates. Solvent response, spectral dimensionality, quantum yield and delayed-fluorescence kinetics each add a different ordering, and no host is best on every axis. A thermal screen would therefore advance precisely the most excitationsensitive material. We replace the stability score with a four-axis descriptor vector—environment, excitation, temperature and time—that keeps each vulnerability visible and lets the intended application decide which tradeoff is acceptable, before a material is committed to devices.

item.title: Microbial Pyrolysis for the Sustainable Synthesis of Nanoparticle-Embedded Carbon Electrocatalysts
item.description: Electrocatalytic processes are essential for a sustainable global economy, yet conventional catalyst synthesis often relies on hazardous reagents and insulating binders that impede performance. Here, microbial extracellular electron transfer for nanoparticle synthesis is integrated with the controlled pyrolysis of microbial monolayers to generate nanoparticle-embedded carbon electrodes. Surface immobilization of Shewanella oneidensis using DNA "Velcro" yields uniform single-microbe-thick layers that are readily patterned and converted into conductive, turbostratic carbon films at temperatures between 800 °C and 1,100 °C. These bio-derived films exhibit progressive graphitic ordering and reach a minimum sheet resistance of 1.49 kΩ/sq, approaching the performance of pyrolyzed synthetic photoresists. Moreover, by leveraging the intrinsic biosynthetic capabilities of S. oneidensis, 3-5 nm palladium nanoparticles are formed directly on the cell surface and seamlessly integrated into the carbon matrix upon pyrolysis. These composites reduce the hydrogen evolution reaction overpotential by 100 mV. This bottom-up bioengineering approach is anticipated to enable the sustainable, programmable fabrication of next-generation electrocatalysts for diverse energy conversion applications.

item.title: Construction of a Curated Literature Dataset and Machine Learning-Guided Exploration of Supported Metal Catalysts for Low- to Intermediate-Temperature Reverse Water–Gas Shift Reaction
item.description: Literature-derived results on reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) catalysts contain extensive information about catalyst design, yet their fragmentation makes systematic, data-driven exploration difficult. Here, we establish a framework that connects a curated RWGS literature dataset to interpretable machine-learning (ML) models and a flexible catalyst-search algorithm. We compiled 607 experimental records from 42 publications on supported metal and metal oxide catalysts evaluated at 300–450 °C, integrating catalyst compositions, preparation and reaction conditions, and CO yields. By systematically comparing nine regression algorithms and nine input representations, we obtained mean cross-validated test R2 values of 0.80, 0.73, and 0.58 for models optimized for the full, 300 °C, and 400 °C datasets, respectively. SHAP analysis identified compositional and experimental features contributing to model predictions, while leave-one-out validation exposed substantial prediction errors in some literature records. In offline sequential-search simulations repeated 100 times, ML-guided search identified high-yield literature entries more efficiently than random selection. Importantly, our newly developed Local-search algorithm jointly explored elemental combinations, loadings, support materials, and experimental conditions without exhaustive enumeration, generating candidates beyond the compositions represented in the training data. The 300 °C search favored Pt–Na/ZrO2-containing candidates, whereas Pd–Na/CeO2-containing candidates predominated at 400 °C. Although these predictions await experimental validation and some violate RWGS equilibrium constraints, this integrated framework provides a reusable data resource and a practical route from accumulated literature knowledge to testable catalyst-design hypotheses.

item.title: Three-dimensional fluorescence lifetime imaging of a molecular rotor at complex interfaces of grease
item.description: Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) maps local physicochemical properties with a confocal laser-scanning microscope. Soft materials are promising targets for FLIM because they demand multi-scale microanalysis; of particular interest are the interfacial properties of complex fluids. However, within each pixel, interfacial and non-interfacial FLIM signals are mixed, which complicates the physical interpretation of FLIM results at interfaces. Here, we propose a systematic FLIM approach: acquire three-dimensional FLIM data at near-diffraction-limited resolution, identify the mixing mechanism by phasor analysis, and perform pixel-level mono- or bi-exponential fitting according to that mechanism. As a proof of concept, we apply this approach to the complex interfaces of grease, in which tens-of-nanometer-scale thickener fibers form a three-dimensional network in the base oil. We prepare a grease labeled with a molecular-rotor dye whose fluorescence lifetime is coupled to the oil viscosity. Three-dimensional FLIM reveals that the lifetime significantly increases at the fiber–oil interfaces. Phasor analysis shows that this lifetime heterogeneity originates from a binary mixture of free-oil and fiber-bound states. Pixel-level bi-exponential fitting then separates the FLIM images into two state maps. In the fiber-bound state, the intramolecular rotation of the dye is arrested, indicating that the oil is solid-like rather than viscous at the interfaces. Beyond the ~180 nm resolution of our images, the lifetime-domain separation resolves the coexistence of the two states within a single diffraction-limited voxel. Finally, we generalize our approach so that FLIM can be broadly applied to map interfacial properties in soft complex materials.

item.title: Sulfotransferase Catalyzed Resolution and Nucleophilic Substitution of Alcohols to Access N-H-Heterocycles
Intermeshed Diphenylacetylenes with Axial Rotation Restricted by Intramolecular Donor–Acceptor Interactions
item.description: Diphenylacetylene (DPA) rotates almost freely around the acetylene axis with rotation mainly restricted by steric repulsion or covalent tethers. We report intermeshed diphenylacetylenes, in which bent π-conjugated units attached to DPA termini cause two donor–acceptor pairs to overlap with each other on opposite sides of the axis. Density functional theory calculations showed that a twisted, stacked conformation with a 36–40° dihedral angle was the most stable for all four molecules. The estimated P/M interconversion barriers (12.8–21.4 kcal/mol) increased with donor and acceptor strength. Upfield shifts in 1H NMR spectra and long-wavelength absorption bands assigned to intramolecular charge-transfer transitions indicated that the stacked conformation predominated in solution. Because rotation was restricted rather than fixed, the molecules exhibited dynamic axial chirality. In a derivative bearing pyridyl groups as acceptors, acid–base interaction with (+)- or (–)-camphorsulfonic acid biased the P/M equilibrium and gave mirror-image induced circular dichroism spectra.

item.title: Surfactant-Toolkit and SurfBench-200: an open computation toolkit and a benchmark of tool-augmented language-model reasoning in surfactant science
item.description: Language models are increasingly used as research assistants in chemistry, but their quantitative work insurfactantscience hasnotbeen measured.We introduce Surfactant-Toolkit, an MIT-licensed Python library and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with 123 validated tools for micellization, mixed micelles, adsorption, emulsions, micelle structure and transport,andSurfBench-200,200graduate-levelquestionswhosereferenceanswersare computed by the toolkit and graded field by field by deterministic scripts. Without tools, five frontier models passed 52.5% to 66.0% of the questions; with the toolkit, the four models run in both conditions passed 92.0% to 98.5% (exact McNemar p < 0.0001 for each), and the open-weightDeepSeek (92.0%) outscored every modelwithouttools.Remaining failures shifted from wrong magnitudes tochoices ofmodelorconvention:toolslargely remove calculation errors, not errors of judgement. Asked the same questions again, every model changed some answers and at least once stated something the data did not support. Used for new findings, the toolkit and two augmented models produced five results on seven research problems that we could not find in the literature. Used for error finding, it showed that five recent papers each contain a value or conclusion that does not follow from their own printed data, from a reversed interaction-parameter sign to a physically impossible molecular area; two frontier models given the same values recomputed nearly all of these without tools but called an undetermined result contradicted. item.title: Redox-Active Leaving Group Enables the Deoxygenative Arylation of Unactivated Aliphatic Alcohols by Thermal, Homogeneous Iron(I)-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling
item.description: Aliphatic alcohols were installed with proposed leaving groups for reaction with well defined, 1,3-diketiminesupported (NacNac)iron(I)-(η6-PhMe) metalloradical, indicating a redox-active 2-isoquinolinyl ether substrate to undergo reductive homolytic C(sp3)–O bond cleavage concomitant with alkyl radical generation as determined by PBN spin trap. The optimal isoquinolinyl ether was employed as substrate in Kumada cross-coupling catalyzed by 10 mol% (NacNac)iron(II) chloride, yielding the deoxygenated, arylated product following homolytic C(sp3)–O β-scission. Hexenyl radical clock experiments and catalyst speciation determined by 19F NMR spectroscopy were consistent with intermediacy of alkyl radicals captured by (NacNac)iron(II)–monoaryl resting state, accessing deoxygenated cross-coupled products derived of naturally occurring aliphatic alcohols such as β-sitosterol and isosorbide.

item.title: A Zwitterionic Indylene with Ambiphilic Redox Reactivity
item.description: Extending transition-metal-like organometallic redox chemistry to indium remains a challenge in molecular main-group chemistry. Here, we report a zwitterionic indylene supported by an anionic bis(N-heterocyclic carbene)borate ligand that displays diverse redox reactivity. Computational and structural analyses reveal a relatively narrow HOMO–LUMO gap together with a stabilizing arene–In interaction involving a vacant indium p orbital, endowing the In(I) centre with complementary donor and acceptor character. This ambiphilicity is expressed experimentally through coordination and reactivity, with a broad range of bond-forming and redox processes, including cycloaddition and the direct oxidative addition of unactivated aryl–halogen bonds. These results expand the accessible reactivity of molecular In(I) and establish bis(NHC)borate ligands as a powerful platform for the development of indium redox organometallic chemistry.

item.title: Formation Energy is All You Need
item.description: A Pourbaix diagram maps which species of an element (metal, ion, oxide or hydroxide) is thermodynamically stable in water as a function of potential and pH, at fixed temperature, pressure and composition. Constructing one requires the Gibbs energies of formation of the participating phases and species. Obtaining reliable values, however, remains difficult: competing phases and species can differ by only a few kilojoules per mole, while published compilations may disagree and are not always freely reusable. Density functional theory (DFT) offers an alternative, but its errors can exceed the energy differences that determine phase stability. We introduce pourbase, an open, source-linked thermodynamic database with a Python package and desktop application for constructing Pourbaix diagrams. Individual reported values, their provenance and a configurable selection policy are accessible and configurable to users even while the database expands as agent-guided literature searches collect new data. We show that replacing a single formation energy can substantially change a predicted stability region and that established thermodynamic compilations can yield conflicting oxide stability boundaries. By making thermodynamic data accessible, traceable, and revisable, pourbase enables reproducible Pourbaix diagrams built directly from experimental evidence, as well as a platform for benchmarking computed values, as we demonstrate for the Materials Project, against experimental values. Ultimately, accurate phase stability predictions need not depend on increasingly complex models, but on getting the formation energies right.

item.title: Influence of divalent cations on the adsorption of DNA origami nanostructures at TiO2 surfaces
item.description: The controlled adsorption of DNA origami nanostructures (DONs) at oxides surfaces is an important step in many applications, ranging from lithographic patterning to sensor fabrication. It is usually facilitated by divalent cations, which screen electrostatic repulsion between the DONs and the surface and may even form salt bridges that firmly immobilize the adsorbed DONs. Here, we investigate DON adsorption at TiO2(110) surfaces mediated by Mg2+, Ca2+, and Sr2+. DON surface coverage is found to increase with cation species in the order Mg2+ < Ca2+ < Sr2+, while cation adsorption at the TiO2(110) surface follows the opposite trend. At the same time, these three cations interact differently with DNA. While Mg2+ undergoes strong coordinative binding with the backbone phosphates, Sr2+ shows weaker binding and forms a large ion cloud around the DNA duplex. Exposing the adsorbed DONs to EDTA leads to the chelation of the bound cations and thus to rapid DON denaturation. However, even for complete DON denaturation, the denatured scaffold remains adsorbed at the TiO2 surface, which suggests that electrostatic repulsion between DON and the surface is overcompensated by additional attractive interactions such as van der Waals interactions. Our results thus provide new insights into the complex interplay of cation-DNA, cation-surface, and DNA-surface interactions and their roles in DON adsorption at TiO2 surfaces, which may result in surprising and counterintuitive behaviors.

item.title: Exploiting Carboxylate Effects to Enhance Cp*CoIII-Catalyzed C–H Functionalization
item.description: Carboxylates are ubiquitous additives in Cp*CoIII-catalyzed C–H functionalization, yet their influence on catalyst speciation and catalytic performance remains poorly understood. Herein, we demonstrate that carboxylate choice can markedly improve reaction efficiency, particularly for substrates bearing weakly coordinating directing groups. Combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and reaction optimization, we identified mesitoic acid (MesCO2H) as an effective additive for hydrogen isotope exchange (HIE), outperforming conventional carboxylates. We then examined the influence of mesitoate and acetate on Cp*CoIII speciation, isolating the corresponding dinuclear complexes. Catalytic studies in HIE revealed that both dimers are catalytically competent, but their activity depends on carboxylate identity and substrate coordination ability, with the mesitoate derivative exhibiting higher activity toward weakly coordinating substrates. We also report the first crystal structure of a direct analogue of the mononuclear κ2-carboxylate Cp*CoIII species proposed as a putative intermediate prior to C–H activation. The isolated mesitoate-bridged dimer enabled C–H deuteration of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals and proved effective beyond HIE in three distinct C–H functionalizations. Together, these findings highlight that carboxylate selection can play a decisive role in fine-tuning Cp*CoIII catalysis, offering new opportunities for rational reaction optimization. KEYWORDS: Cp*CoIII catalysis; C–H activation; catalyst speciation; carboxylates

item.title: Multi-Scale Continuum Modeling of Mediated Electron Transfer in 3D Living Bio-Anodes
item.description: Bioelectrochemical systems, in which electroactive microbes transfer electrons across biological-abiotic interfaces, represent a vital technology for sustainable energy production, chemical synthesis, and environmental remediation. However, these systems are constrained by a two-dimensional design paradigm, with reactors achieving power densities 10–100-times lower than theoretical limits because conventional architectures restrict electron transfer to a single layer at the electrode surface. Here, we establish quantitative design rules that govern three-dimensional bio-electrochemical function driven by small-molecule electron transfer mediators. Through integrated theory, simulation, and engineered biofilm validation, we identify two distinct scale-dependent transport regimes: a macroscopic regime where bulk mediator availability governs active layer expansion and a microscopic regime where microbial packing geometry controls local redox cycling, both of which are fundamentally constrained by mass transport. We validate these scaling laws experimentally using agarose-encapsulated Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 and demonstrate that rational mediator loading and cellular packing can elevate current densities beyond 0.5 A m-2, exceeding two-dimensional performance ceilings. These design principles provide a generalizable blueprint for engineering high-performance biocatalytic systems and offer researchers studying natural biofilms a mechanistic framework to decode internal transport architecture.

item.title: ETALON: Verified Execution and Persistent Research Memory for Agentic Computer-Aided Drug Design
item.description: Language-model agents can coordinate computational drug discovery, but adapting a campaign to new evidence requires scientific software that supports flexible workflows, consistent modeling, and continuity across research sessions. Here we present ETALON, a harness that equips a general-purpose coding agent with an integrated environment for computer-aided drug design. Three independently usable systems supply its scientific operations: MolQuarry for chemical and biological evidence, MolCascade for molecular preparation, screening, and docking, and PRISM for molecular generation and physical modeling. Each exposes configurable procedures with explicit scientific requirements, so the host can revise its research strategy while retaining consistent preparation and evaluation practices. Operations registered with a common execution layer are checked before dispatch, and their outputs carry separate records of completion, verification, and admission, so that an incomplete computation is not recorded as an unfavorable molecular result. A persistent research graph links evidence, judgments, experiments, and results across sessions, and candidate method revisions are compared with frozen baselines under criteria declared in advance.

item.title: Impact of Electrochemical Doping on the Excited State Decay of 2H-MoSe2 Nanosheets
item.description: Colloidal 2H-MoSe2 nanosheets combine solution processability with electronic properties attractive for photocatalytic water splitting, yet the electrochemical stability of the excited state remains poorly understood. We combine potential-modulated absorption spectroscopy and complementary electrochemical methods with transient absorption spectroscopy to investigate charge injection and excited-state dynamics in few-layer 2H-MoSe2 nanosheet films. We determine the electron affinity, ionization potential and exciton binding energy and predict an overpotential of +0.6 V for the photocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction. Prolonged exposure to electrochemical operating conditions reduces the lifetime of the excited state, which scales with the overpotential, and which is particularly pronounced under anodic conditions. Our work establishes absorption spectroelectrochemistry as a powerful probe of colloidal transition-metal dichalcogenides and identifies solution-processable 2H-MoSe2 nanosheets as promising photocathode components for S-scheme heterostructures.

item.title: From Photo-crosslinking to Covalent: A Cascade DNA-Encoded Library Strategy for Pin1 Inhibitor Discovery
item.description: Peptidyl-prolyl cis–trans isomerase NIMA-interacting 1 (Pin1) plays vital biological roles in vivo and has been studied as a therapeutic target for a variety of human diseases. Covalent inhibitors represent the mainstream strategy in current Pin1 drug discovery, however, existing covalent molecules still rely on known affinity scaffolds or direct screening. Herein, we developed an innovative cascade DNA-encoded library (DEL) strategy that integrates photo-crosslinking with covalent targeting, enabling the de novo design of novel Pin1 covalent inhibitors. Photo-crosslinking DEL (PDEL) selection was first used to identify low-affinity binding fragments. These fragments then served as the beginning for covalent focused DELs (Co-FDEL) construction. Finally, covalent DEL selection led to the identification of two hits, LWH-1 and LWH-2, which covalently modify Pin1 at Cys113, with IC50 values of 447.4 nM and 273.7 nM. This strategy facilitates the rational evolution of low-affinity fragments to potent covalent inhibitors, offering an accelerated pathway for targeting challenging proteins.

item.title: Insights into the formation of 3-Methyl-2-butene-1-thiol in Cannabis sativa flowers through the identification of its glutathionylated and cysteinylated precursors
item.description: Odor emissions from cannabis cultivation have been described as “skunky”, a sensory characteristic recently associated with the compound 3-methylbut-2-ene-1-thiol (3MBT). However, the biosynthetic origin of this key odor-active compound in Cannabis sativa remains unknow.
